section_summary: This section begins with translated 1941 correspondence from the Tokyo branch of Petróleos “Leon” concerning secret Japanese purchases in Mexico of molybdenum, mercury, copper, oil, special steel, and other strategic materials, together with disputes over prices, payments, and Mitsubishi and military involvement. The 1942 material includes public correspondence about prewar American exports to Japan and British economic-warfare assessments of Japan’s leather supply and the economic weaknesses of its occupied territories, especially shortages of textiles and markets for Southeast Asian raw materials. The final documents discuss Abraham Z. Phillips’s Japanese dealings, his placement on the proclaimed list, and renewed but disputed investigations of mercury smuggling from Mexico.

subfiles.title: Letter from Fuminaga Fujii to Abraham Z. Phillips concerning molybdenum and consignment goods (continuation)
subfiles.from: Fuminaga Fujii, Tokyo branch of Petróleos “Leon” S.A.
subfiles.about: Fujii urges Phillips to ship contracted molybdenum and warns him about Japanese Navy and Mitsubishi efforts to force down the prices of consigned strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Fujii argues that Showa Tsusho and Ando remain responsible for the prepaid molybdenum contract and that delivery is essential to preserve the branch’s standing with Major General Ishikawa and the Army. He describes conflicts with Mitsubishi and the Navy over special-steel prices, warns that Joseph may pressure Phillips after obtaining further shipments, and reports that the cargo of the Heiyo Maru is being sorted at Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Summary of letter from Fuminaga Fujii to Abraham Z. Phillips
subfiles.about: The summary reports disputes over the value and handling of high-speed steel and other consignments sent from Mexico to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fujii says Japanese buyers found some supposed high-speed steel to be low-grade carbon steel and that Japan needed cobalt, vanadium, and nickel rather than imported high-speed steel. He describes hostility from Mitsubishi and the Navy, Army interest in oil and other materials, and the Tokyo branch’s efforts to protect and inspect the shipments. Because censorship was tightening, he requests secret communications through Fujita of NYK while keeping Nagamatsu in the background.

subfiles.title: Letter from Fuminaga Fujii to Abraham Z. Phillips urging shipment of molybdenum
subfiles.about: Fujii demands performance of the prepaid molybdenum contract and separates the Mitsubishi consignment account from an earlier Manchukuo payment.
subfiles.summary: Fujii states that $134,300 had been paid through Showa Tsusho for 100 tons of molybdenum but no shipment had occurred, damaging the branch’s credibility with the Japanese military. He complains that Phillips had ignored inquiries for copper, mercury, asbestos, gasoline, crude oil, and lubricants and attributes his secrecy to Joseph’s financing. Fujii also asks for $10,000 in operating funds and insists that Mitsubishi’s disputed $90,000 Manchukuo payment must not be combined with the Navy’s $250,000 consignment fund.

subfiles.title: Letter from Fuminaga Fujii to Sanshiro Nii about shipments, pricing, and communications
subfiles.about: Fujii answers accusations of incompetence, reviews the handling of several cargoes, and renews his appeal for delivery of molybdenum.
subfiles.summary: Fujii rejects Nii’s criticism of the Tokyo branch and attributes delays to inflated invoices, unsuitable special steel, and the great difference between Mexican asking prices and Japanese official prices. He says Kobayashi should settle the Mitsubishi consignments in Mexico and explains why Ando was later used as a liaison despite initially being dismissed as a mere messenger. The letter emphasizes the Army fuel plant’s urgent need for molybdenum, denies that the $134,300 payment should be applied to consignment goods, and asks that confidential communications be concealed from Kobayashi and Yamaguchi.

subfiles.title: Letter from Y. Nagamatsu to Abraham Z. Phillips on pending strategic-material transactions
subfiles.about: Nagamatsu reviews the Tokyo branch’s outstanding Navy, Army, Mitsubishi, and Showa transactions shortly before the Pacific War.
subfiles.summary: Nagamatsu urges Phillips to secure additional funds from Joseph, settle the Mitsubishi and Showa consignments, and ship even small quantities of molybdenum—or substitute mercury or electrolytic copper—to the Japanese Army. He reiterates that Mitsubishi’s $90,000 Manchukuo payment is separate, proposes a major future oil transaction, and describes a clandestine diplomatic channel through the Salvadoran consul to evade censorship. The letter also reports Fujii’s Army summons and demands strict secrecy because Navy officials were calling the branch disloyal.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese economic gains in Malaya
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file containing a British memorandum on Japan’s principal economic gains in Malaya.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies a despatch from Great Britain associated with Somerville and concerning Japanese gains in Malaya of economic value. It points to file 740.00112 Pacific War/36 for the original paper.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. J. McNeil to Sumner Welles about criticism of prewar trade with Japan
subfiles.about: An Idaho legislator requests information with which to answer criticism that the Roosevelt administration sold scrap iron and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McNeil encloses an Idaho Daily Statesman clipping connected with disputes over the prewar isolationism of Senator John Thomas and Representative Henry Dworshak. He asks for details about congressional positions on trade with Japan so that he can defend the President and State Department in the press and on the platform.

subfiles.title: Idaho Daily Statesman clipping: “Keep Pitching, Bill!” and letter to the editor
subfiles.from: Vardis Fisher and J. R. Collard
subfiles.about: The clipping combines an appeal for better tobacco supplies for servicemen with a letter defending prewar isolationist votes and criticizing exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vardis Fisher argues that tobacco is a necessity for troops and condemns bureaucratic buck-passing over cigarette supplies for American forces in Australia. J. R. Collard’s adjacent letter objects to attacks on Idaho isolationists, claims earlier rearmament and termination of scrap, gasoline, and munitions sales to Japan might have changed the war, and urges support for the criticized congressmen.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on the history of trade restrictions against Japan
subfiles.about: The Department supplies a chronology of American economic measures against Japan from 1938 through 1941.
subfiles.summary: The reply recounts the moral embargoes prompted by bombing of civilians, discouragement of credit, termination of the 1911 commercial treaty, and the introduction of export licensing after July 1940. It lists restricted metals, fuels, and machinery and explains that the July 1941 freezing of Japanese assets effectively ended trade after Japan moved into southern Indochina. A copy of Roosevelt’s July 24, 1941 remarks is enclosed to explain the wider diplomatic and military considerations.

subfiles.title: Telegram from London on machinery and automotive-parts information
subfiles.about: Winant reports that the Ministry of Economic Warfare has not yet completed a requested study of machinery and automotive parts.
subfiles.summary: The telegram responds to the Department’s August 11 request for information intended for the Board of Economic Warfare. It promises that the Ministry’s study will be forwarded when completed.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5282 transmitting the memorandum “Japan—Leather”
subfiles.from: James Somerville, United States Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Somerville transmits a British estimate of Japanese leather production and possible surplus supplies for Germany.
subfiles.summary: The despatch says Japan and its occupied territories might theoretically furnish Germany about 13,000 tons of leather content, equivalent to roughly 10,000 tons of dry hides. It cautions that reports of military footwear shortages suggest Japan was failing to exploit conquered territories at anything like their normal surplus levels. Copies were distributed to economic, military, naval, and strategic-intelligence offices.

subfiles.title: Ministry of Economic Warfare memorandum “Japan—Leather”
subfiles.about: The memorandum estimates Japan’s leather requirements and the potential leather surpluses of territories under Japanese control.
subfiles.summary: The analysis estimates Japanese output at about 30,000 tons annually and possible current requirements near 40,000 tons, with military demand likely to rise if the war extended to Siberia. It calculates nominal surpluses of 53,000 tons across Japan, Manchukuo, Korea, China, and occupied Southeast Asia, leaving a conjectural 13,000-ton surplus for Germany if Japan could exploit all areas fully.

subfiles.title: Letter from H. C. Lohse to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Lohse challenges Grew to explain why the United States continued supplying Japan with strategic materials before Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.summary: Lohse accuses American war profiteers of helping build Japanese strength and asks what Grew had done during his decade as ambassador to warn the country. He argues that stopping scrap exports five years earlier might have reduced Japan’s military capacity and asks Grew for the facts.

subfiles.title: Reply from Maxwell M. Hamilton to H. C. Lohse
subfiles.about: Hamilton defends Grew’s reporting and explains the legal basis and timing of American export restrictions against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton assures Lohse that Grew and the Tokyo embassy reported Japan’s economic, political, and military position to Washington. He explains that Congress did not grant authority to restrict defense-related exports until July 1940, after which licenses for scrap iron, aviation gasoline, metals, machine tools, and other strategic goods were progressively denied. Roosevelt’s July 24, 1941 remarks are enclosed for further context.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on weaknesses in Japan’s conquered areas
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends reading London despatch No. 5602 on Japan’s inability to supply or purchase adequately within its conquered territories.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes the despatch’s thesis that Japan could neither supply manufactured goods, especially textiles, nor buy the raw materials produced in occupied regions. It predicts falling living standards and growing discontent in those territories and recommends the full despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5602, “Weaknesses in Japan’s Position in Conquered Areas”
subfiles.from: James Somerville, United States Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Somerville analyzes the structural economic weaknesses of Japan’s empire and transmits supporting press and DNB material.
subfiles.summary: The despatch treats Japanese claims of making oil from surplus Malayan rubber as propaganda intended to reassure populations deprived of normal export markets. It argues that occupied Southeast Asian economies produced large raw-material surpluses but depended on imported manufactured goods that wartime Japan could not adequately supply. Particular emphasis falls on cotton-textile shortages, unfavorable exchange and trade terms, declining living standards, labor shifts, and the likelihood of unrest exploitable by anti-Japanese propaganda.

subfiles.title: Enclosure of DNB dispatches on Japanese economic plans in Asia
subfiles.about: Four German-language dispatches describe Japanese monetary, transport, production, textile-export, and trade plans for occupied Asia.
subfiles.summary: The reports outline use of the military yen, transport integration, raw-material development, agricultural restructuring, and continued concentration of heavy industry in Japan. Additional dispatches describe reduced textile quotas for Thailand, proposed changes in Southeast Asian production and Japanese exports, and Hishinuma’s warning that wartime trade would not expand substantially for perhaps two years. The individual reports are dated July 30, August 5, and August 19, 1942.

subfiles.title: Financial Times clipping, “Japanese Oil from Rubber Plan—Claims Discredited”
subfiles.about: The article disputes Japanese propaganda claiming that Malayan and East Indies rubber could provide oil on a commercially significant scale.
subfiles.summary: London experts argue that rubber-to-oil technology was old, inefficient, costly, and dependent on chemical plant, labor, coagulants, and plantation facilities that Japan lacked in the occupied regions. Although low-temperature carbonization could yield small fractions of motor spirit, diesel, and fuel oil, even the theoretical maximum would be minor beside Japan’s needs. The article concludes that Japan probably had ample captured petroleum and that Allied blockade strategy should focus on distribution and preventing shipments to Germany.

subfiles.title: Strictly confidential letter from George S. Messersmith to Philip W. Bonsal on Phillips and mercury
subfiles.about: Messersmith evaluates Grew’s evidence about Phillips’s Japanese trade and warns against reopening settled investigations of Mexican mercury exports.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith says Phillips had traded strategic metals and scrap with Japan but apparently stopped when Mexican and American law made the business illegal, and he stresses that the Japanese ultimately left Phillips with losses. He questions keeping Phillips on the proclaimed list when comparable American traders suffered no such disability. Messersmith also argues that Mexico’s exportable mercury was reaching the United States and dismisses claims of substantial clandestine shipments to Germany as fantastic.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on Abraham Z. Phillips’s reputation and blacklisting
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics staff
subfiles.about: The memorandum disputes a favorable view of Phillips and considers how Bonsal should answer Ambassador Messersmith’s recommendation to remove him from the black list.
subfiles.summary: The writer characterizes Phillips as a naturalized Mexican of Polish Jewish origin who had served as a Japanese purchasing agent and participated in questionable oil ventures. It also alleges that he planned to buy a high-octane gasoline cracking plant in the United States for shipment to Japan through Mexico. A draft response was prepared because Messersmith’s removal recommendation faced opposition in the interdepartmental proclaimed-list committee.

subfiles.title: Letter from George S. Messersmith to Philip W. Bonsal on renewed mercury inquiries
subfiles.about: Messersmith reports that the Board of Economic Warfare has reopened questions about mercury smuggling from Mexico and complains about duplicative wartime investigations.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith links the new inquiry from Dr. Bateman to possible reports from military or naval intelligence or to Grew’s Gripsholm despatch, much of which the embassy already knew and had acted upon. He sends Bonsal a copy of his reply to Bateman and notes that Ransom could supply the needed information in Washington. The letter ends by criticizing poorly substantiated rumors from numerous agency investigators as a waste of time and effort.
